Brightens the whole frame by 1/3 stop with no other change. Used for batch-correcting underexposed frames or matching a bracket to its neighbours.
Darkens the whole frame by 1/3 stop with no other change. Used for batch-correcting overexposed frames or matching a series shot with drifting exposure.
Brightens the whole frame by 2/3 stop with no other change. Used for batch-correcting underexposed frames or matching a bracket to its neighbours.
Darkens the whole frame by 2/3 stop with no other change. Used for batch-correcting overexposed frames or matching a series shot with drifting exposure.
Brightens the whole frame by 1 stop with no other change. Used for batch-correcting underexposed frames or matching a bracket to its neighbours.
Darkens the whole frame by 1 stop with no other change. Used for batch-correcting overexposed frames or matching a series shot with drifting exposure.
Brightens the whole frame by 2 stop with no other change. Used for batch-correcting underexposed frames or matching a bracket to its neighbours.
Darkens the whole frame by 2 stop with no other change. Used for batch-correcting overexposed frames or matching a series shot with drifting exposure.
Pulls highlights to -25 to regain sky, white clothing or window detail, with whites at +0 so the image keeps a bright top end. Stack with exposure steps for blown but recoverable raw files.
Pulls highlights to -50 to regain sky, white clothing or window detail, with whites at +0 so the image keeps a bright top end. Stack with exposure steps for blown but recoverable raw files.
Pulls highlights to -75 to regain sky, white clothing or window detail, with whites at +8 so the image keeps a bright top end. Stack with exposure steps for blown but recoverable raw files.
Pulls highlights to -100 to regain sky, white clothing or window detail, with whites at +12 so the image keeps a bright top end. Stack with exposure steps for blown but recoverable raw files.
Opens shadows by 25 to reveal detail in backlit faces, interiors and under hats, with blacks at +0 to keep some depth in the darkest tones. A fill-light utility for contrasty scenes.
Opens shadows by 50 to reveal detail in backlit faces, interiors and under hats, with blacks at +0 to keep some depth in the darkest tones. A fill-light utility for contrasty scenes.
Opens shadows by 75 to reveal detail in backlit faces, interiors and under hats, with blacks at -6 to keep some depth in the darkest tones. A fill-light utility for contrasty scenes.
Opens shadows by 100 to reveal detail in backlit faces, interiors and under hats, with blacks at -10 to keep some depth in the darkest tones. A fill-light utility for contrasty scenes.
Raises global contrast by 10 as a clean step, for flat raw files that need more separation without a colour or curve change.
Lowers global contrast by 10 as a clean step, for harsh midday files or to prepare a frame for grading.
Raises global contrast by 20 as a clean step, for flat raw files that need more separation without a colour or curve change.
Lowers global contrast by 20 as a clean step, for harsh midday files or to prepare a frame for grading.
Raises global contrast by 35 as a clean step, for flat raw files that need more separation without a colour or curve change.
Lowers global contrast by 35 as a clean step, for harsh midday files or to prepare a frame for grading.
Sets the black point 10 lower so shadows reach a true black. Check the clipping warning (hold Alt while dragging Blacks) and stop where only a few specks appear.
Raises the black point by 10 for a lifted, print-safe or faded shadow floor, useful for matte output and subtitles over dark areas.
Sets the black point 20 lower so shadows reach a true black. Check the clipping warning (hold Alt while dragging Blacks) and stop where only a few specks appear.
Raises the black point by 20 for a lifted, print-safe or faded shadow floor, useful for matte output and subtitles over dark areas.
Sets the black point 30 lower so shadows reach a true black. Check the clipping warning (hold Alt while dragging Blacks) and stop where only a few specks appear.
Raises the black point by 30 for a lifted, print-safe or faded shadow floor, useful for matte output and subtitles over dark areas.
Raises whites by 10 to bring the brightest tones toward white. Hold Alt while dragging Whites and stop when the first colour appears so highlights do not clip.
Lowers whites by 10 to keep specular highlights and bright paper white inside printable range.
Raises whites by 20 to bring the brightest tones toward white. Hold Alt while dragging Whites and stop when the first colour appears so highlights do not clip.
Lowers whites by 20 to keep specular highlights and bright paper white inside printable range.
Low-contrast starting point for grading in another tool or for heavy colour work: neutral profile, compressed highlights, lifted shadows and a gentle black floor.
Flat starting point with colour also held back, so a colourist can push saturation selectively without the file clipping first.
Flat start for portrait grading: neutral profile, protected skin highlights and open shadows, with no mixer change.
Flat start for landscape grading: deep highlight recovery for skies, strong shadow lift, neutral profile.
Flat monochrome start with full tonal range, for toning or contrast shaping later.
Flat start for dark scenes: lifts shadows without opening the whole frame and holds whites down, for nightlife or stage work headed to grading.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under a candle, oil lamp or low sun at sunrise, about 2000 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under a household bulb, about 2750 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under a standard incandescent bulb, 3000 K as camera makers set it. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under photographic tungsten and halogen, 3200 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under sodium vapour street lamps, about 2700 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under warm white LED, 2700 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under neutral white LED, 4000 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under cool white LED, 5000 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under daylight LED, 6500 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.

Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under warm white fluorescent tube, 3000 K, with a small magenta tint to offset the green spike. Tint +8. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.

Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under white fluorescent tube, 3700 K, with a small magenta tint to offset the green spike. Tint +8. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.

Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under cool white fluorescent tube, 4200 K, with a magenta tint to offset the green spike. Tint +10. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.

Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under day white fluorescent tube, 5000 K, with a magenta tint to offset the green spike. Tint +10. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.

Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under daylight fluorescent tube, 6500 K, with a magenta tint to offset the green spike. Tint +10. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under high temperature mercury vapour, 7200 K, with a magenta tint. Tint +12. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under low-angle sunlight, about 4000 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under direct sun, 5200 K as camera makers set it. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under summer noon sun, about 5600 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under electronic flash, 5400 K as camera makers set it. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under cloudy sky, 6000 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under snow scenes under a grey sky, about 7000 K. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Sets absolute white balance: for raw files shot under open shade, 8000 K as camera makers set it. Tint +0. It replaces the as-shot value, so use it only on raw files, not JPEG.
Black and white with the mixer left flat, like unfiltered panchromatic film. The reference against which filter looks are judged.
Classic first-choice yellow filter: slightly darkens blue sky so clouds lift out, keeps skin natural and separates greens. The most subtle filter look.
Yellow filter with firmer contrast for mixed landscapes: darker blue sky, bright clouds and clearly separated foliage tones.
Orange filter: stronger than yellow, milder than red. Sky goes distinctly dark with strong cloud contrast. A general landscape and architecture favourite.
Orange filter for portraits: warm tones lighten for smooth skin, freckles and blemishes recede, lips and background blues drop away.
Red filter at half strength: dark sky, bright clouds and lightened warm subjects without full storm drama.
Red filter at full effect: blue sky near black, sharp clouds, red flowers separated from foliage. Strongest look of the classic set, suited to stormy scenes.
A deep red or infrared-like rendering: very dark sky, bright warm tones and pale foliage contrast. Keep exposure headroom in the highlights.
Green filter: lightens leaves, including dark ones that would otherwise go black, and separates foliage from flowers and buds. Specialist plant look.
Green filter that also lightens the sky, for forest scenes where leaf detail matters more than sky drama.
Blue filter: lightens blues and darkens warm colours, which exaggerates haze and mist for a calm, atmospheric mood.
Softer blue-filter look that keeps distant ridges and fog bright and lets warm foreground subjects fall dark.
Light sepia that tints shadows only (hue 35, saturation 20) and leaves paper-white highlights clean. A restrained antique look.
Mid-strength sepia in the 25 to 40 hue range with shadow and midtone tint, the familiar brown print.
Sepia with warm yellow highlights and slightly raised blacks, imitating a print that has yellowed over time.
Dense dark-brown sepia with more shadow saturation and a firm contrast curve for portraits and still life.
Selenium toning at its reddish-brown end: hue near 350, saturation about 22, in shadows and midtones for deeper blacks with a subtle warm tint.
Selenium toning toward the purple end of its range, with a cooler plum shadow tint on a neutral highlight.
Stronger selenium look with more shadow saturation and deeper blacks, as used for archival fine-art prints.
Cyanotype in Prussian blue, with saturation 60 in shadows against 15 in highlights and balance pushed to +55 so the result blends.
A pale, sun-washed cyanotype with lower saturation and lifted blacks, like a lightly exposed contact print.
Dark, saturated cyanotype with strong blue shadows and contrast, for dramatic architecture or botanical studies.
Soft platinum print: very low-contrast warm grey with a long tonal scale and lifted blacks.
Cooler platinum-palladium interpretation, with a neutral-to-cool shadow cast and gentle roll-off.
Brown-black platinum tone with a visible warm tint through the midtones, for portraits and landscapes with an old-print feel.
Classic split tone: highlights hue 50 and shadows hue 220, both at moderate saturation, with a small balance toward highlights.
A quiet version of amber and blue split toning, for B&W that reads neutral at a glance and warm to cool on inspection.
Cool blue shadows with orange highlights that suit skin, for B&W portraits that need a hint of life.
Gold highlights over cool ink-blue shadows, a richer print tone for low-key still life.
Cross-process style split: green-blue shadows and red-orange-yellow highlights over a colour image.
Capture sharpening for portraits: radius 1.2 for the larger scale of faces, detail kept low and masking high at 70 so skin stays smooth while eyes, lashes and hair edges sharpen.
Portrait sharpening for crisp studio work: slightly higher amount with masking at 60 to protect skin texture from harshness.
Gentle sharpening for older or textured skin: low amount, low detail, masking 80 so only the strongest edges are sharpened.
Landscape capture sharpening: small radius 0.8 for fine detail, detail at 40 to bring out texture and low masking at 25 so the whole frame sharpens.
Sharpening for leaves and grass: radius 0.8, high detail 50 and moderate masking so textures pop without haloing branches against sky.
Landscape sharpening with masking at 55 so clear sky and water gradients are not roughened while rock and horizon edges sharpen.
Sharpening for lines and facades: radius 0.9, detail 25 for clean edges, masking 40 to avoid noise in flat walls and sky.
Macro capture sharpening: small radius 0.7, detail 45, masking 35. For insects, petals and fabric at close range.
Product sharpening: radius 0.8 and detail 30 with masking 40, so edges are crisp and plain backdrops stay clean.
Food sharpening with radius 1.0 and moderate detail so crusts and garnishes show texture without a crunchy look.
Street and reportage sharpening: radius 1.0, detail 35, low masking so grain and texture read as part of the look.
Sharpening for fur and feather: radius 0.9, detail 40, masking 40 to keep out-of-focus backgrounds smooth.
The values Adobe uses in its sharpening tutorial: amount 85, radius 1.0, detail 25, as a general starting point for a slightly soft raw.
Moderate sharpening with masking at 55 for files that were just denoised, since noise reduction softens detail and heavy sharpening brings the grain back.
Sharpening for on-screen use: smaller radius 0.8 and light amount, for images exported at 2048 px or less where fine edges would otherwise soften.
Screen sharpening for detail-heavy images: radius 0.6 and detail 35, to survive downsizing without a crunchy edge.
Print sharpening for glossy and lustre paper: radius 1.2 and amount 60, lighter than matte because smooth paper keeps detail.
Print sharpening for matte, fine-art and canvas: larger radius 1.5 and amount 75 to cut through paper texture. Start here and adjust from a test print.
Large-format print sharpening viewed from a distance: radius 1.8, low detail so grain and noise are not amplified.
Phone sensors are tiny, so even base ISO needs clean-up. Light luminance 15 and colour 30, with detail kept high.
Phone files at ISO 400 to 800: luminance 30 with colour 35 and smoothness 55 to calm mottled shadows.
Night-mode and high-ISO phone files: luminance 45 and colour 45, detail lowered to 35 to remove blotchy chroma noise.
Small sensor compacts at low ISO: luminance 10, colour 25 (Adobe's default), for a clean look with full detail.
Small sensor compacts at ISO 800 to 1600: luminance 25, colour 30, a balance between grain removal and fine detail.
Small sensor compacts at ISO 3200 and above: luminance 40, colour 40, detail 35 to keep sky and shadows smooth.
Micro Four Thirds at moderate ISO: luminance 20 and colour 28, tuned for the roughly one stop noise penalty of the smaller sensor.
Micro Four Thirds at high ISO: luminance 35, colour 35, detail 40, contrast 10 to keep edges readable.
APS-C at base to moderate ISO: light colour reduction at Adobe's default 25 and no luminance, since the files are already clean.
APS-C at ISO 800 to 1600: luminance 15, colour 25, detail 50.
APS-C at ISO 3200 to 6400: luminance 30, colour 30, detail 45, contrast 5, for events and indoor sport.
APS-C at extreme ISO: luminance 50, colour 40 and smoothness 60, accepting some softness for a usable file.
Full frame at low to moderate ISO: noise reduction mostly off, only the default colour value of 25.
Full frame at ISO 1600 to 3200: luminance 10, colour 25, keeping fine detail intact.
Full frame at ISO 6400: luminance 25, colour 28, detail 50, contrast 5.
Full frame at very high ISO: luminance 40 (a figure used in published workflows for ISO 25600), colour 30 and contrast 10.
Medium format at base to moderate ISO: no luminance reduction and colour at 20, preserving the format's fine detail.
Only colour noise reduction at Adobe's defaults (colour 25, detail 50, smoothness 50): a safe start that leaves luminance grain and detail alone.
Stronger colour smoothing for purple or green blotches in skies and shadows: colour 40, smoothness 70, with colour detail lowered to 40.
Fine, soft grain (amount 14, size 17, roughness 57) like a slow film, adapted from a published ISO 400 example. Adds a trace of texture to clean digital files.
Fine, tight grain with lower roughness, for a sharp slow-film feel on landscapes and architecture.
Very light, fine grain for colour work (amount 10): enough to break banding in smooth skies and gradients.
Medium grain at the amount of about 20 that many educators start from, with default roughness 50 for a mild natural texture.
Medium grain with high roughness for a soft, rounded, mid-speed film look.
Medium grain with low roughness for a more noise-like, gritty digital-meets-film texture.
Coarse, soft grain for a fast-film look in colour: larger size, high roughness, moderate amount.
Coarse grain at default roughness, for documentary and street frames shot to look like pushed film.
Heavy, large grain (amount 50) for stylised work. Larger sizes work best in B&W, so pair with a monochrome edit.
B&W with a large, visible grain (amount 50, size 71, roughness 50) from a published black and white example, for street and reportage.
Fine monochrome grain that gives a silvery texture without noise, for portraits and fine-art prints.
A very light corner brightening (amount +10) with wide feather, to open dark edges on a portrait or product without being noticed.
A gentle light vignette (amount +22) that lifts edges for a high-key, airy frame.
A barely visible darkening (amount -8) with very wide feather, the kind a viewer does not notice but that holds the eye.
Gentle edge darkening (amount -15) with a wide, smooth feather, for portraits and travel frames.
Medium edge darkening (amount -25) with midpoint 45, to focus the eye on a centred subject.
Strong vignette (amount -40) with a firmer feather of 60, for dramatic portraits and moody scenes.
Heavy tunnel vignette (amount -55) for a stylised or vintage treatment. Use sparingly.
Oval vignette (amount -22, roundness -30) following the shape of a vertical portrait.
Wide landscape vignette (amount -18, roundness -20) that darkens the corners and sky edges for a natural framing.
Medium vignette (amount -25) with highlights at 60 to protect bright skies and windows from going muddy at the edges.
Light purple fringe removal (amount 4) for small edges around bright branches and windows. Increase amount only after the lens profile CA fix.
Medium purple defringe (amount 8). Purple fringing tends to appear in front of the focal point on contrasty edges.
Strong purple defringe (amount 14) for fast lenses shot wide open against bright skies. Watch for desaturated purple flowers and clothes.
Light green fringe removal (amount 4), for green edges behind the focal point.
Medium green defringe (amount 8) for backlit foliage and rooflines.
Strong green defringe (amount 14) for severe green edges. Check foliage next to the fringe for dulling.
Both fringe colours at amount 6, a general clean-up for contrasty edges when the culprit colour is unclear.
Both fringe colours at amount 12 for badly corrected wide-angle or telephoto lenses at high contrast edges.
Shifts the red channel scale by -20 to tackle red-cyan lateral chromatic aberration visible towards the frame edges.
Shifts the red channel scale by +20 for lenses where the red-cyan fringe runs the other way.
Shifts the blue channel scale by -20 for blue-yellow lateral chromatic aberration.
Shifts the blue channel scale by +20 for blue-yellow lateral chromatic aberration running the other way.
Small corrections to red (-10) and blue (+10) for lenses with mixed fringing, applied after checking at 200% on a high contrast edge.
Light lens vignetting correction (+15) to open corners on wide-open zooms where the profile is unavailable.
Stronger lens vignetting correction (+35) for fast primes shot wide open.

For items shot on white: raises exposure and whites so the backdrop approaches white while shadows stay open, then keeps the product's own colours untouched. Check the backdrop clip and limit it before export.
White-background look that keeps a soft contact shadow: whites open but blacks and shadows unchanged, so objects stay grounded.
Light grey seamless: slightly lifted exposure, clean neutral and low saturation hold, for catalogue consistency across a batch.
Neutral mid grey backdrop with firm midtone contrast, for apparel and accessories where a white sweep would blow out light items.
Charcoal backdrop with lifted product highlights and a slight shadow roll-off, for electronics and watches.
Colour-accurate base: neutral profile, no mixer change and no creative grading. The principle is correction, not embellishment, so returns stay low.
For bright plastics and neons that capture flat: modest saturation and vibrance, with a clamped gain so the colour matches the item in hand.
White metal jewellery: brighter whites, a cool-leaning neutral, higher micro-contrast on facets and a light sharpen. Keeps highlights below clip so shine reads as metal.
Gold and rose gold: keeps yellows and oranges rich but not orange-brown, with controlled highlights so metal does not blow out.
For cut stones: higher contrast and texture bring out facets, a touch of vibrance keeps stone colour true, and blacks are held so reflections stay dark.
Clothing flat lays and ghost mannequins: texture and clarity for weave, neutral colour, and open shadows in folds.
White shirts and linens: highlights pulled to hold weave, whites raised to reach clean white, and low saturation to stop colour casts.
Black and navy items: shadow lift of 35 recovers seams and texture, and blacks are held so the garment stays black.
Glass products: strong highlight control for reflections, boosted micro-contrast on rims and a clean neutral background.
Black plastics and screens: gentle shadow lift and texture to show matte surface, highlights tamed so edges stay defined.
Wood, leather and craft goods: warm-leaning orange saturation balance with texture and clarity for grain, in a neutral colour space.
Food by window light: soft contrast, protected highlights and gently open shadows, with texture and clarity kept modest so the food looks real.
Overhead daylight table scenes: firm contrast and crisp texture with neutral whites.
Flat overcast light: adds contrast and a touch of warmth to the mid tones to bring depth back to a dull set.
For dishes lit by kitchen bulbs and shot with the warm cast baked in: cools midtones and highlights and pulls orange down, without touching white balance.
Corrects the green-yellow cast of tube-lit dining rooms with a magenta wash, then lifts skin and sauce tones back to warm.
Dim restaurant tables: lifts shadows, calms noise, keeps the warm lamp mood but protects the bright plate.
Asian dishes: richer reds and oranges for chili, soy and glaze, steady greens for herbs, and local contrast to show sheen.
Pasta and pizza: saturated tomato red, bright basil green, soft cream tones in the dough.
Bread and pastry: a warm golden crust, protected cream interior and texture to show crumb and flaky layers.
Barbecue and roasts: deep browns, bright sauce reds, and local clarity for char, without muddy shadows.
Salads and vegetables: crisp, lively greens with clean whites, and a light vibrance lift.
Fish and raw dishes: neutral whites, protected pink and orange flesh, and controlled specular highlights on wet surfaces.
Cakes and confectionery: bright, airy and slightly desaturated pastels with soft contrast.
Chocolate, coffee and dark sauces: deep brown tones with highlights held and shadows lifted, for visible gloss and texture.
Fruit and drinks: vivid yellows, oranges and reds with clean whites, and vibrance rather than flat saturation.
Curries and spice markets: deep yellows and warm reds, with local contrast for sauce texture and a restrained green.
Colourful street and table food: strong but controlled reds, greens and yellows, with extra contrast for lively garnish.
Interiors with bright windows: strong highlight and whites reduction, lifted shadows and dehaze, so the view outside reads while the room stays open. Pair with a bracket merge for extreme scenes.
Bright airy listing look: exposure up about a stop, highlights down 70, shadows up 80, contrast down 20 and vibrance up 15, matching a published bright and airy example.
Natural designer style: modest brightening, soft contrast, kept colour and a little texture on wood and fabric.
Neutral white walls and ceilings: cooler mid-tones to neutralise warm lamp spill, whites open, mixer reducing orange.
Cosy evening interiors with lamps on: keeps the warm lamp glow but protects bright bulbs and opens dark corners.
Basements and small rooms with little daylight: large shadow and exposure lift with noise reduction and held blacks.
Hardwood floors and cabinetry: richer orange, texture for grain, and protection against orange-red glow.
White kitchens: bright neutral cabinetry and counters (grey counters should read neutral), highlights pulled so glossy surfaces keep detail.
Wood cabinets and stone counters: warm but not orange, texture for grain, with under-cabinet shadow lift.
Bathrooms: cool white tiles and fixtures, glare held down, cleaner whites and a mild texture on grout and stone.
Sunny exteriors: tamed highlights on white trim, open shadows under eaves, richer blue sky and greener lawns.
Grey day exteriors: brightens, adds contrast and a little sky separation to a flat scene.
Lawn and landscaping: deeper but natural greens, a controlled yellow, and clearer foliage detail.
Dusk exterior: boosts window warmth and luminance, lowers siding exposure, and warms the highlights, for a blue hour sky with a glowing house.
Deeper blue hour look with a darker cyan-blue sky and warm interior glow, for premium listings.
Concrete and brutalist forms: heavy texture, strong contrast, desaturated grey tones and darkened sky separation.
Glass curtain walls: cool, crisp reflections, controlled highlights and mild dehaze so sky and glass separate.
Brick and terracotta: richer warm tones, deeper shadows and texture for mortar lines.
Old stone, churches and monuments: texture and mild clarity for carved detail with natural warm-grey tones.
White modern buildings: bright, clean, low saturation, with highlight protection so white surfaces keep their form.
Interior architecture: open shadows, controlled windows and gentle clarity for shape of vaults and stairs.
Hazy skylines: dehaze 25, local contrast and darkened sky to cut through atmospheric haze.
Blue hour city: deeper blue sky, warm window lights and a lifted shadow floor.
Steel structures and industrial sites: cool grey metals, high local contrast and desaturated colours with pops of rust.
Warm, low sun on historic facades: golden tones, balanced shadows and a light clarity for relief and carving.
Overcast architectural records: neutral rendering, lifted contrast and gentle dehaze to avoid flat greys.
For the top 5 m (about 15 ft) where red is just starting to fade: mild warm shift in midtones, a touch of red in the calibration and balanced contrast.
At 5 m about 90 percent of red is gone: stronger warm grade in mid and shadows, red calibration shift toward orange and higher saturation, and dehaze for clarity.
Past 10 m orange is also essentially gone, so this adds warmth and more red hue shift, lifts shadows and dehazes. Works best on raw with a manual white balance or strobes.
Past 20 m yellow also fades, leaving a cold green-blue cast. Strongest warm grade and magenta wash to cancel green, for ambient light frames.
Green coastal or lake water: a magenta wash cancels the green cast, greens and aquas are calmed, and warmth returns to the subject.
Open ocean blue: keeps blue deep and clean while protecting skin and fish colours, with a gentle haze cut.
Wide-angle frames with surface light: warm top highlights, strong blue shadows, local contrast for beams.
Macro and nudibranchs: vivid saturated subject colours with controlled blue background and fine detail.
Silvery fish and divers: neutral highlights, contrast for reflective bodies and a little dehaze, without unnatural colour.
Surface and snorkel frames at 0 to 3 m: very light warm shift and low haze, since little red has been lost yet.
Wrecks and caves: lifted shadows, strong dehaze and cleaned colour for rust and murk.
Pool shots: cools down cyan, keeps skin warm and calms specular glare, for swim sport and portraits.
Rooms lit by daylight windows and warm lamps: cools the lamp-lit midtones and warms shadows so the two sources sit closer together. Correct the priority subject first, then mask the rest.
Event halls with tungsten, LED and daylight together: a mild magenta-cool wash, a calmer orange, and neutral highlights.
Light fix for fluorescent green: nudges mid and highlight tones toward magenta (similar to a tint of +5 to +15) and reduces green and yellow saturation.
Strong green cast from tube lighting or cheap LED: bigger magenta wash and stronger green desaturation.
Small magenta cast fix: mid and highlight tones are moved toward green, as a light Tint-left correction would do.
Strong magenta or purple cast, such as shaded foliage or a sensor shift: bigger green counter-wash and reduced magenta saturation.
Warm-yellow cast from old lamps or dirty filters: blue wash on mids and highlights with calmer yellows.
Cool blue cast from shade or an overcast sky: warm wash on mids and highlights, softer blues.
Cyan or teal cast, from reflected water or screens: red-orange counter wash and reduced cyan saturation.
Orange-green street lamp cast: cool blue-magenta counter wash with calmer oranges, for night street frames lit by sodium lamps.
Skin gone red, green or magenta under stage or coloured lamps: gently centres orange and red hue with a restrained saturation fall.
Green bounce on faces and clothing under trees: magenta counter wash in midtones with calmer greens, while keeping the skin warm.
Soft north window light on the bride and dress: protects white dress highlights, opens shadows, keeps skin neutral. Set white balance on the dress first.
Detail shots of the gown, lace and veil: keeps whites clean without clipping and brings out fabric texture.
Close detail of rings, bouquet and invitations: gentle contrast and colour so petals and metal read clearly.
Interior with warm room lamps and a window: pulls orange cast off skin and walls using grading and mixer, no white balance change.
Natural, slightly crisp colour for the groom and groomsmen getting dressed: neutral skin, firm contrast, dark suits kept detailed.
Flattering soft treatment for candid group moments during hair and makeup, with low texture on skin and gentle highlights.
Close portraits during makeup: even skin, gentle lip and eye colour, tamed redness from warm lamps.
Bounced on-camera flash in a dim room: cools the slightly yellow ceiling bounce, lifts shadows, keeps skin natural.
Church interior with coloured window light on pews and walls: calms blue and red patches and recovers bright windows.
Dim church lit by warm lamps: cools the orange wash with grading and keeps candlelit warmth in the highlights.
Window light mixed with ceiling fixtures: evens colour casts across the frame by tempering yellow and orange saturation.
Ceremony under trees or a canopy: warms cool shade lightly, lifts shadows and keeps greens natural.
Hard midday sun at an outdoor ceremony: recovers white dress highlights and dark suits, tames saturated greens.
Emotional vows and tears, tight shots of faces: softened texture, gentle contrast and warm skin.
Walking the aisle with a bright door behind: lifts the bride's face from the backlight and holds dress detail.
Joyful exit shots: bright, lightly saturated colour with a touch of contrast for confetti and petals.
Evening ceremony with candles: keeps the warm glow, lifts faces without flattening the mood, controls noise.
Faithful, unstyled colour for clients who want it just as it looked: neutral contrast, accurate skin, no grade.
Accurate colour with a clean, slightly warm skin rendering for indoor ceremonies in cool light.
Film-inspired ceremony base: gentle matte curve, muted greens and warm highlights, light grain.
Low-key ceremony look for dim venues: deeper shadows, protected highlights, desaturated colour, cool shadows.
Direct on-camera flash at a reception: tames shiny highlights on faces and brings back warmth.
Bounced flash with ambient tungsten: removes the green or orange bias in skin while keeping venue warmth.
